problem: Existing VLA navigation models assume reasoning and control are temporally aligned: they either block execution during slow VLM inference or consume stale semantic outputs as if they were current. Dual-system designs decouple the two but still treat inference latency as negligible, so policies trained under synchronous supervision degrade under real latency.
motivation: On mobile robots with limited compute, VLM inference takes seconds while control runs at tens of Hz, and in dynamic human-centric scenes stale semantics become misaligned with the world. The authors argue latency is a modeling problem, not just an engineering one, and should be exposed to the policy and matched between training and deployment.
key_idea: Expose delayed VLM semantics (KV cache) plus explicit latency and ego-motion-offset metadata to a fast action policy, and train it with injected reasoning delays in both imitation learning and online RL.
insight: KV-cache features plus latency awareness together give the best result (SR 47.06 vs 16.47 for waypoint interface without latency, 30.59 for KV cache without latency). Ego-motion offset helps (SR 41.18 to 47.06), and RL under injected delay makes the policy more robust across latency settings. Blocking synchronous inference drops SR to 32.94, versus 47.06 for the asynchronous no-RL variant. The ablations suggest that simple query-based policies beat diffusion and flow policies, and that a mid-sized VLM (1B) balances capacity against latency.
method: Delayed semantic-control interface: the action policy conditions on the last-layer KV cache of the VLM computed from frames at t-Δt, plus latency Δt and accumulated ego-motion offset (Δx,Δy,Δθ), so it can reinterpret stale semantics in the current frame.

Dual-system asynchronous execution: InternVL3-1B (InternViT-300M + Qwen2.5-0.5B) reasons at about 0.5 Hz on frames at offsets {0,3,6,9}s; the action expert runs at 10 Hz, never blocks, and reuses the cached KV. The vision encoder is shared.

Query-based action expert: six cross-attention Transformer layers where 30 learnable time queries attend to current visual tokens, projected KV cache, and robot state and latency tokens. An MLP outputs 3 s of (dx,dy,dθ) increments that are integrated into a trajectory.

Stage 1, VLM SFT: full-parameter fine-tuning with the vision encoder frozen on GPT-5-annotated long-horizon instructions and structured CoT reasoning (critical objects, motion, progress, next plan) plus waypoints, mixing reasoning and waypoint-only targets.
Stage 2, IL under delay: delays Δt~U(0,10)s are sampled to build delayed KV/latency inputs from synchronous demonstrations, trained with a smooth-L1 loss on integrated poses.

Stage 3, PPO with asynchronous guidance: only the action policy is fine-tuned (final cross-attention layer + MLP decoder), with the VLM frozen. Random delays averaging about 5 s are injected in a dynamic Isaac Lab environment, with a reward for goal, progress, collision, and speed.

DynaNav benchmark: Isaac Sim/Lab suite with 4 scenes (hospital, office, warehouse, outdoor), dynamic pedestrians (up to 200), wheeled Nova Carter and Spot robots, teleoperation data collection, parallel RL training, and 85 test episodes.

setting.backbone: InternVL3-1B (fine-tuned) VLM + Transformer cross-attention action expert (IL then PPO)
setting.training_data: SCAND (8.7 h), GND (11+ h), DynaNav sim teleop data (310 episodes, 5.1 h); GPT-5 generated instructions and CoT annotations; online PPO in DynaNav sim
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB (current frame plus frames at -3/-6/-9 s for the VLM) and robot velocity state
setting.action_space: continuous relative motion chunks (dx,dy,dθ) over 3 s (30 steps), converted to linear/angular velocity commands

numbers.extra: async VLM at 0.5 Hz, action policy 10 Hz; baselines fine-tuned on same data

numbers_note: Latency-robustness results are only in a figure (not extracted). The paper's main table has one row per method on DynaNav (85 episodes, single split, no official split names). Real-world SR is a fraction from 5 trials per task. The appendix reports success threshold 1.5 m, while the main text says 1 m.
results: On DynaNav, TIC-VLA reaches SR 55.29, SPL 50.29, CR 28.24, beating NavDP (SR 54.12, which uses point-goal privileged info) and clearly beating DualVLN (30.59), NaVILA (28.24), and Uni-NaVid (22.35). In the real world on a Go2, it reaches 0.85 SR on an RTX 4060 and 0.75 on a Jetson Orin NX under multi-second latency, versus 0.50 for DualVLN and 0.35 for NaVILA on an A6000.
limitations: Evaluation is on the authors' own small benchmark (85 episodes, 4 scenes) and a small real-world test (5 trials per task), with no standard VLN benchmarks.
Reasoning at about 0.5 Hz with multi-second delay still limits performance; the model is small (1B) and depends on GPT-5 annotations and simulation RL.
Only navigation with a frozen VLM during RL; extension to manipulation is left to future work.
